title: Who Is Nithya Raman? The Kerala-Born Urban Planner Who Just Became Los Angeles' First Indian-American Mayor
excerpt: Born in Thrissur, raised between Kerala and Massachusetts, trained at Harvard and MIT, Nithya Raman mapped Chennai's missing services, organised Los Angeles neighbours around homelessness, unseated two incumbents six years apart — and on December 14 becomes the first Asian American, Indian American and Hindu mayor of America's second-largest city.
body:
• Nithya Varsha Raman, 45, the Kerala-born urban planner who has represented District 4 on the Los Angeles City Council since 2020, defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in the November 3, 2026 election. She takes office on December 14 as the city's 44th mayor — its first Asian American, first Indian American and first Hindu mayor, according to her biographical record.
  • Raman's route to City Hall ran through Harvard and MIT, work with slum communities in Delhi, the civic-data initiative Transparent Chennai, which she co-founded in 2010, and the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, the Los Angeles homelessness outreach group she co-founded in 2017.
  • She won her council seat in 2020 as the first challenger in 17 years to unseat a sitting Los Angeles councilmember, was re-elected outright in the March 2024 primary, and built her council record on renter protections, rent caps and oversight of homelessness spending.
  • With New York led by Zohran Mamdani, who took office in January 2026, South Asian Americans will now run the two largest cities in the United States. Los Angeles County officials are scheduled to certify Raman's win on November 27; her four-year term begins December 14, with the 2028 Summer Olympics ahead.

On November 3, Los Angeles chose change over incumbency. Nithya Raman — born in Thrissur, Kerala, raised partly in Thiruvananthapuram, and carried to the United States at the age of six — defeated Mayor Karen Bass, the former congresswoman who in 2022 became the first woman to lead the city. USA Today reported that Raman won by about four percentage points in the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's results, in the first defeat of a sitting Los Angeles mayor since 2005. Bass conceded on November 5, saying she had called Raman to congratulate her and was committed to "ensuring a smooth and seamless transition." The result remains unofficial until certification, scheduled for November 27.

"Here in Los Angeles, this election is about change, too. A city that was engineered over the last few decades to resist change, and the people right here who said enough is enough."

— Nithya Raman, to supporters on election night, November 3

Speaking at the Original Farmers Market two days later, Raman placed the win inside the city's immigrant story. "And the idea that Angelenos voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor at this moment in American history is so deeply moving to me," she said, according to IANS. She is a member of the Democratic Party and of the Democratic Socialists of America, and she campaigned — as our coverage of the midterm results noted — in a cycle that returned a string of Indian American winners across the country.

A Thrissur childhood, a Massachusetts adolescence

Nithya Varsha Raman was born on July 28, 1981, in Thrissur, Kerala, into a Tamil Iyer family with roots in both Thrissur and Thiruvananthapuram, according to The American Bazaar. Her father, Venkitaraman, worked at KELTRON, the Kerala state electronics company; her mother, Sudha, worked in banking. Raman spent her earliest years in Thiruvananthapuram, in the care of her maternal grandparents for part of that time, and attended pre-primary classes at Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan before the family left India.

At about six, she flew to join her father in Louisiana; the family later settled in Burlington, Massachusetts. She became a naturalised American citizen at 22, taking the oath in Boston. The Kerala connection did not lapse: The American Bazaar reported that she last visited Thrissur in 2019 for a family function, and relatives in Thiruvananthapuram publicly celebrated her victory this week.

Harvard, Delhi and the making of an urban planner

Raman studied Social Studies at Harvard University, graduating in 2003. The housing question found her early: at Harvard she joined a programme providing interest-free loans to tenants facing eviction, and a freshman-year roommate recalled her sleeping outside in freezing weather to draw attention to homelessness, The Harvard Crimson reported via IANS. "The Housing Opportunities Programme was a big influence for me in thinking about insecurity for people, and what can we do to help stabilise people during difficult moments in their lives," she told The Crimson.

After Harvard she worked in India with organisations supporting slum communities in Delhi, against evictions and for basic services. "Seeing how the government decisions negatively impacted the lives and livelihoods of so many made me realise how important urban governance was. That pushed me to study urban planning," she said in a 2020 interview quoted by IANS. She earned a master's degree in city planning at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2008. Her thesis adviser there, Balakrishnan Rajagopal, later described her political career as following a "straight line" rooted in housing and the lives of marginalised people.

She then returned to India and in 2010 co-founded Transparent Chennai, a civic-data initiative under the Centre for Development Finance that mapped urban poverty and basic infrastructure — down to whether public toilets were actually located near the slum settlements whose residents needed them, as The Global Indian recounts. The project treated data itself as a public service: information the city did not collect, or did not share, gathered and published so residents could hold it to account.

Los Angeles: staffer, organiser, councilmember

Raman moved to Los Angeles in 2013 and joined the office of the city's Chief Administrative Officer, examining how public money was spent on homelessness; IANS reported that she found much of about $100 million had gone towards arrests rather than housing, outreach or services. In Silver Lake, where she settled, she co-chaired the neighbourhood council's homelessness committee and in 2017 co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, a volunteer organisation providing food, clothing and healthcare assistance and connecting people on the streets with shelters and housing. She also served as executive director of Time's Up Entertainment.

Volunteering convinced her that community effort alone could not match the scale of the problem, and in 2020 she challenged District 4 councilmember David Ryu. A volunteer army knocked on more than 83,000 doors. Raman won the November runoff with 52.9 percent of the vote — the first challenger in 17 years to unseat a sitting Los Angeles councilmember, and the first South Asian and first Asian American woman to serve on the council. The Los Angeles Times called the result a "political earthquake."

On the council she chaired the Housing and Homelessness Committee from 2023 and built a record around tenants and rents. In 2021 she helped advance amendments widening the city's tenant harassment ordinance to cover cash buyout offers and threats to report false information to law enforcement. Legislation she supported extended just-cause eviction protections to about 400,000 additional rental units, according to city figures reported by the Los Angeles Times. In November 2025 the council approved her proposal to lower annual rent-increase limits for rent-stabilised apartments — home to nearly half the city's residents — from a 3–8 percent range to 1–4 percent depending on inflation, the first strengthening of the rent stabilisation ordinance in 40 years. She was re-elected in March 2024 without a runoff, winning 50.6 percent in the primary against 38.6 percent for her nearest opponent.

A bid filed hours before the deadline

Raman's mayoral campaign began as a rupture. She had endorsed Bass for re-election weeks earlier; on February 7, 2026, hours before the filing deadline, she filed to run against her. Nine council colleagues reaffirmed their support for Bass. Raman told NBC4, in remarks reported by USA Today, that she was running because Los Angeles was "not delivering on the basics at a time when the public has trusted us with hundreds of millions of dollars to solve complex problems like our housing crisis and our homelessness crisis."

She finished second in the June primary, overtaking reality television personality Spencer Pratt for the runoff place only as mail ballots were counted. Through the autumn she campaigned on increasing housing production, improving basic city services, more oversight of homelessness spending — she described Bass's Inside Safe programme, which moves people from encampments into temporary accommodation, as fiscally unsustainable — and reviving a film industry whose contraction she has watched at home: her husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, whom she met at Harvard, is a television writer with credits including "Modern Family" and "30 Rock," and she recused herself from several council votes on streamlining film production to avoid a conflict of interest. She has said she will sign an executive order on her first day to speed up housing approvals. The Los Angeles police union spent more than $5 million opposing her, The 19th reported, citing campaign finance records.

The case her critics will keep making

Raman takes office with her record under the same scrutiny she applied to others. Bass's campaign pointed to her votes on Los Angeles Police Department hiring amid concerns about staffing levels. On homelessness, the record she defended as "oversight and accountability" included a rental-voucher programme that aimed to house 600 households by July 1 but had placed three by then and 54 by August 13, according to figures reported by the Los Angeles Times; in August, the council presidency split the housing and homelessness committee she had chaired. She cited a 49 percent decline in street homelessness in her own district even as homelessness rose again citywide, a trend USA Today noted had reversed two years of declines. How she answers those numbers, at city scale, is now the job.

Why her win reaches beyond Los Angeles

For the Indian diaspora, the arithmetic of this November is striking on its own. With Raman in Los Angeles and Zohran Mamdani — the son of filmmaker Mira Nair and scholar Mahmood Mamdani — in New York, "South Asian Americans will lead the two largest cities in the United States," as Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, put it in congratulating her. The organisation noted that California's South Asian community numbers more than 1 million residents. Raman lives in Silver Lake with Chandrasekaran and their twins, Karna and Kaveri.

Her first term will be measured quickly. She has described hers as "one of the shortest transitions across the country — for a city of 4 million people where the challenges are absolutely immense," and Los Angeles must also prepare to host the 2028 Summer Olympics. The planner who once mapped Chennai's missing toilets now owns Los Angeles' hardest list: homelessness, housing supply, basic services and public safety. She asked for the job on a single argument — that the city can deliver on the basics. On December 14, the delivery starts being graded.
